issues.legal_issue: A transfer of a minor’s immovable property by a natural guardian without the required prior permission is voidable, not void, and must be set aside before the minor can recover the property from the transferee.
material_facts: The minors’ mother, acting as their natural guardian, sold portions of their immovable property without obtaining prior court permission.
The courts found that the sales were not supported by legal necessity.
The plaintiffs sought possession from the purchasers while initially asserting that the transfers were void and could be ignored.
issues.conclusion: The transfers were voidable at the instance of the minors, so the plaintiffs had to obtain an order setting them aside before claiming recovery of the transferred property.
issues.legal_principle: Section 8(2) of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956 prohibits a natural guardian from transferring a minor’s immovable property by sale without previous court permission. Section 8(3) expressly makes a disposal in contravention of that requirement voidable at the instance of the minor or a person claiming under the minor. No earlier cases are relied on.

predicates.suit_seeks_recovery_under_guardian_trans: A claimant brings a civil suit seeking to recover property transferred by a guardian of a minor.
predicates.natural_guardian_sold_minor_immovable_pr: A natural guardian sold a minor’s immovable property without obtaining the permission required for that sale.

issues.definition: When a recovery suit concerns a sale by a natural guardian without required permission, the transfer is voidable and must first be set aside.

issues.legal_issue: Adding a prayer to set aside a guardian’s transfer is not a mere formality when the original suit treated the transfer as void; if the amendment changes the basis of the suit, the claim to set aside the transfer is treated as filed when the amendment is made.
material_facts: The original plaint sought recovery and treated the guardian’s sales as void from their inception, without seeking that they be set aside.
The plaintiffs later amended the plaint to add a prayer to set aside the sales.
The added prayer changed the basis of the claim from treating the sales as void to seeking to avoid the guardian’s transfers.
issues.conclusion: The claim to set aside the sales was treated as filed on the date the amendment was allowed, rather than on the date the original plaint was filed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court distinguished a claim based on an assertion that a transaction is void from a claim seeking to set aside a voidable transfer. Because the amendment changed the basis of the suit, it was not a merely formal addition and the relief was treated as sought from the date of amendment. No statute or earlier case is cited for this pleading principle.

rule.if: civil_suit_seeks_to_avoid_guardian_transfer and original_pleading_treats_transfer_as_void and later_amendment_adds_setting_aside_prayer and amendment_changes_basis_of_claim

predicates.civil_suit_seeks_to_avoid_guardian_trans: A claimant brings a civil suit seeking to avoid a transfer made by a guardian.
predicates.original_pleading_treats_transfer_as_voi: The original pleading asserts that the transfer was void and could be ignored, rather than seeking an order to set it aside.
predicates.later_amendment_adds_setting_aside_praye: The claimant later amends the pleading to request that the transfer be set aside.
predicates.amendment_changes_basis_of_claim: The amendment changes the claim from treating the transfer as void to seeking to avoid a transfer that is voidable.

issues.definition: When an amendment adds a setting-aside claim and changes a suit’s basis from treating a transfer as void to seeking to avoid it, that claim is treated as filed on the amendment date.

issues.legal_issue: A ward’s claim to set aside a guardian’s transfer is barred if it is brought more than three years after the ward attains majority.
material_facts: One plaintiff attained majority more than three years before the suit was filed.

The other plaintiff filed the original suit within three years after attaining majority, but the prayer to set aside the transfers was added by amendment more than three years after attaining majority.
The claim to set aside the transfers was treated as filed on the amendment date because the amendment changed the basis of the suit.
issues.conclusion: The setting-aside claims were out of time: one was already late when the suit was filed, and the other was late when the setting-aside relief was added by amendment.
issues.legal_principle: Article 60 of the Limitation Act prescribes three years for a ward who has attained majority to set aside a transfer of property made by the ward’s guardian, running from the date the ward attains majority. Applying the rule that the amended setting-aside claim was filed on the amendment date, the Court held that the relevant period had expired. No earlier cases are relied on.

predicates.ward_claims_to_set_aside_guardian_transf: A person who was a minor brings a civil claim to set aside a transfer made by the person’s guardian.
predicates.more_than_three_years_elapsed_since_majo: The claim to set aside the transfer is filed more than three years after the claimant attains majority.

issues.definition: A ward’s claim to set aside a guardian’s transfer is barred when it is filed more than three years after the ward attains majority.
